utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone in and just outside the courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-84-T, the Prosecutor versus Ramush Haradinaj et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Di Fazio, I see -- is Mr. -- yesterday, I asked whether there was any objection against D27, D28, D29, or D30. MR. DI FAZIO: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections? MR. DI FAZIO: No --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then -- MR. DI FAZIO: -- if Your Honour would give me a moment, one of them had to be kept - I think it might have been a Prosecution exhibit - had to be kept under seal. I just need to check Mr. Re's e-mail, but other than that there's no problem. That's right, our only concern was P30, which has to remain under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D30, proofing notes. Any objection against that having admitted under seal?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think Mr. Di Fazio was referring to P30, rather than D30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, he said so. Yes. Mr. Di Fazio, but I take it that in view of D30 -- yes -- MR. DI FAZIO: I just wanted to convey no problems with the Defence exhibits, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll check carefully whether the Defence exhibits -- perhaps you would like to check that as well, Mr. Emmerson, to see whether there's anything in here which is protected.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I will do exactly that. So can we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then after the break, we'll hear from you or later today.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. That's one issue. Then when will the Chamber hear from the Defence whether there's any objection against the, as I say, re-arranged exhibits for Witness Andjelkovic? Because I did understand that it has been re-arranged and that a letter was sent to the Chamber with a copy to Defence teams, 2nd of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, can I again re-visit that after the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Because I'm slightly taken by surprise in relation to it. I probably my fault rather than anybody else's.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it only draws the attention to it now, then the purpose has been served. Then I would like to inform the parties that the Chamber has decided that we will not be sitting on the following days, which are all Fridays, unless - and that's the same condition as we earlier have applied - unless we need parts of these days to conclude a witness's testimony or deal with an urgent procedural matter. So it's not an absolute non-sitting, and, of course, it's difficult to say it many weeks in advance whether we are in such a situation. It would be the 27th of April, 18th of May, 25th of May, and the 8th of June. I think some of these dates were known already, but not all of them. Then, Mr. Di Fazio, are you ready -- is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness? MR. DI FAZIO: I am, but could I just raise two very brief matters?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: They all concern this afternoon and how we go ahead. Firstly, I -- I believe, Your Honours, that the parties and the Trial Chamber was notified that I intended to use a very small excerpt from a video that's been on our exhibit list for some time, and last week we advised that we didn't intend to use any exhibits at all with this witness. So I think I should formally raise that with you and make sure that there's no problems, either from the Defence point of view or from the Chamber's point of view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any problem as far as the Defence is concerned? I see nodding no -- MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- three times. Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. The other issue is this: The next witness -- sorry, not the next witness, the witness after the next witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: -- I spoke to this morning, and the Defence have received proofing notes, or rather, evidence there had been no proofing. Now during the course of this conversation, he expressed to me that he's pretty exhausted and pretty tired. He's a man who's received some substantial injury during the war. And he says that he was reluctant to testify today. I undertook on his behalf to convey those remarks to you. I don't know if the Defence can indicate how long they will be with the next witness, the immediate witness, the one coming up next, I can indicate that I won't be long with him. Now, if it transpires that the Defence are going to be the lion's share of the remainder of the day, Your Honours may care to consider not going past the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: That's all -- that's all I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You would take less than the one and a half hours scheduled? MR. DI FAZIO: It is my earnest intention to take as shortest time possible with this witness. I think -- I am confident it will be under one and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there any indication - of course, it's difficult to forecast - but would you need more than the usual time, that's one and a half hours, same time?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'd expected to be about an hour and a half with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I just raise one other matter in terms of timing and scheduling, in particular in relation to the point that Mr. Di Fazio raises. Obviously, none of us has any desire whatsoever to put a tired witness in the witness box, even for examination-in-chief. Cross-examination of that witness is likely to be comparatively short. The witness to follow, on the other hand, is likely to be considerably longer. Can I just outline the position. It is Witness 8. I had an indication from Mr. Re this morning that - and I won't go into the details if Your Honours will forgive me - but that the Prosecution, for reasons that he will explain or may explain, propose to elicit from Witness 8 a part of his testimony but not the whole of his testimony, as revealed in the statements, which would mean that his evidence-in-chief might be rather shorter than was perhaps anticipated. However, again for reasons I don't wish to go into at the moment, the portion of his evidence that the Prosecution is not proposing to elicit is a portion which we will in due course submit is essential to understanding the witness's reliability and credibility. And so for that reason, it will not in any way shorten cross-examination; indeed, possibly the reverse because it will be necessary to traverse in cross-examination material that would potentially be covered in chief. The reason I'm mentioning now is because if the witness who is about to follow after the present witness does not testify this afternoon and, for example, occupies half of tomorrow's session, there is a danger that we will find ourselves pressurised as to time at the back end of Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand. This Friday there's no possibility for an overflow because it's a UN holiday, so therefore we have no flexibility whatsoever. Mr. Di Fazio, is -- first of all, is there any way of communicating with the Defence what portions the Defence thinks could be more efficiently dealt with in examination-in-chief in order to save a lot of time at a later stage? I invite you to communicate, that might not be all of it, but perhaps certain portions of it, and of course, Mr. Emmerson, only to the extent that you feel free to -- well, to tell Mr. Di Fazio because you're not giving the reasons but that perhaps might not prevent you from identifying those portions you would like to be --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just in case I left myself anything short of clear on this, the witness that I was referring to a moment ago is not the witness that Mr. Di Fazio is referring to but the one to follow on from that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I can certainly communicate to Mr. Di Fazio as regards the witness he is concerned about; that is to say, the gentleman who is tired and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, I was referring to the other one that you --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: There's no scope in relation to the other one for any common ground at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then I've given it a try --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: There is, however, scope for common ground and shortening the evidence-in-chief with the witness who is proposed to be called after the witness who is about to be called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, okay. Then we have -- let's talk about the first witness today and the possible second witness today -- well, let's say the witness who you say has expressed that he is tired. When did he arrive in The Hague, could you tell us? MR. DI FAZIO: He got in last night. My understanding --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So relatively short he is in The Hague, yes. MR. DI FAZIO: He got in -- yes, that's right. But he started his -- it wasn't just a question of getting out of the capital city and going to the local airport, he started a long journey to get to -- from his home to one of our field offices. The trip from his home to the airport started early yesterday, and then it was a long trip from there to Amsterdam.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If, of course, if he would see whether there's a possibility at all to ask the witness to come and testify, that would be later today, most likely not before -- approximately 6.00 and would not take much longer than one hour. Perhaps the VWS could see whether they could give sufficient rest this afternoon to the witness. I don't know whether -- unless there's still any conversations ongoing with him or whether this is time for his own, and then to see whether we could find a situation and we do not lose any further time, because 125 hours has gone by very quickly, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's see whether the witness could be in such a shape that he can -- that he can answer questions during one hour. Let's see whether that's manageable; if not, of course, we'll have to accept that. Then any other matter. MR. DI FAZIO: No, not from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then -- yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I should just alert the Chamber that the witness to follow all the witnesses that we have just spoken about is also a witness who I contemplate will take a considerable period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and that's number 4 in the sequence which will now start?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. That's on the record. Madam Usher, could you -- would you please be so kind as to escort the witness into the courtroom. No protective measures, Mr. Di Fazio, as far as I understand? MR. DI FAZIO: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I expect Mr. Zvonko Markovic to enter the courtroom in a minute? MR. DI FAZIO: I certainly hope so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. While we're waiting, it gives me an opportunity, I think a short message was sent to the parties yesterday about marking of maps, and that was inspired by the experience of yesterday afternoon, too. MR. DI FAZIO: With respect, that's an excellent suggestion, Your Honours. Unfortunately, I may have to refer to some maps this afternoon -- well, a map this afternoon --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes -- MR. DI FAZIO: And I didn't -- obviously, couldn't get back to this man, but in future we will certainly take up the Trial Chamber's suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do not hear any objections from the Defence. Perhaps it's good to have it in full on the record when the witness has not arrived; that is, that markings on neutral matters on maps are made outside the court, and then the marked map be presented in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Markovic, at least I presume that you are Mr. Markovic, before you give evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Madam Usher will now hand out the text. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Markovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You will first be examined by Mr. Di Fazio, who is counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Di Fazio, you may proceed. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, are these details correct: You were born on the 26th of May, 1964, in Decani, and you are of Serb ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: In early 1998, you worked as a postman?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And that was in a small village, and pardon my pronunciation, known as Gornji Streoc or something very similar to that?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Could you, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, could we first confirm the first name of the witness? MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you Mr. Zvonko Markovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: What is the name of the village which just was mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Gornji Streoc. MR. DI FAZIO: S-t-r-e-o-c, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Just a few more details about your occupation. How long had you worked in that place as a postman?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Nine years.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And some more personal particulars, please. Could you tell the Trial Chamber of the names of your siblings, your brothers and sisters; start with the oldest, include yourself, and finish with the youngest.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Sonja, Zvonko, Rade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Three children in your family?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And what was Rade's occupation in the 1990s?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: He was a company manager. It was a trading company in Decani.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'd like you to turn your attention, please, to the early months of 1998. You've told us that you were the postman and that you were working in Gornji Streoc. Did you work there alone or were there other employees working in the post office?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I was a post-master and also an employee, and there was a postman who was delivering mail.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And what was the area of responsibility, so to speak, for this post office; in other words, to what area or, better still, to what villages did your post office provide services to?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: The post, as a building, was in Gornji Streoc. It covered the villages --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slowly enumerate the names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It covered a total of nine villages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you give the names of any villages, would you please do it slowly so that the interpreters can translate. Please proceed. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I don't -- I don't think we actually got the names of the villages, if you can provide them. So if you can provide us with the names of the villages to which you -- your post office provided services, please do so, and do it slowly. Read -- list them slowly.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Gornji Streoc, Ljubisa, Istinic, Papic, Papracani, and Donji Streoc.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Turn your mind back to the first few months of 1998. Were you able to continue working in your role as postman at Gornji Streoc?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Sometime in late March or April, one of my friends from Gornji Streoc with whom I was intensively associated, and his name was Sinan Musaj, told me that it was no longer safe for me to come to the village to work because terrorists had emerged, and that it would be better for me not to come to work anymore for my own safety. I informed about that the authorities, or rather, our head office in Djakovica, and they told me that I had waited too long because a postman had been killed near Pristina, and there was a recommendation and guide-lines issued to all post offices to make their own assessment whether they would continue their services due to safety concerns. With their approval, I closed the post office in Gornji Streoc and moved to the post office in Decani. One counter was allocated to me so that I can continue my work, paying out pensions, deliver letters, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the ethnicity of this gentleman Sinan Musaj?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: He was an Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did he ever provide you with any more details, other than what you've told us, about the terrorists emerging and that it would be better not to come to work any more for your own safety? Did he go beyond that or is that all he said to you?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So I take it that's all he said and you took his advice?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: At the time when you closed the -- the post office, where were you actually living?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: In Decani.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, you've told us that you moved to Decani, and you opened a special counter so that you could continue your work paying up pensions and delivering letters. Now, was that to any specific group of the population or was -- were you providing general services for the area?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I provided services to the general area that I covered in Gornji Streoc, and that applied to all the people who wanted to come and collect their pension or their mail in Decani.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. And just before we leave this topic, you said there had been a recommendation and guide-lines issued to all post offices to make their own assessment as to whether it was safe to continue operating. Did you make that assessment as to whether it was safe to continue Gornji Streoc's post office or did someone else take that decision?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I followed Sinan's recommendation and advice that it wasn't safe. I sought the opinion of my head office in Djakovica, and thereafter I closed the post office.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. And you -- I think you've mentioned this happened in April, but can you be specific about when precisely it was, the closure occurred?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Sometime in April, but I don't know exactly as to the date. Perhaps mid-April, but I'm just guessing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. All right. So you moved to -- or rather, your work-place was set up in Decani, and did you continue to work as a postman in Decani?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I worked there for about a month until I delivered all the pensions and other allowances, and then I was called by the reserve police force. I responded to this call. I closed my counter, and it was taken over by the Decani post office while I joined the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. We just need to clarify a couple of matters there. Firstly, you don't know exactly when it was that you moved from Gornji Streoc to Decani, other than it was sometime in April, but you are sure that you continued for about a month. So you would have continued to work as a postman in Decani at least -- at the very least until early March, possibly later. Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Early May -- MR. DI FAZIO: Oh, May, I'm sorry. I can't -- school's --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Early May?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Roughly speaking, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. And, finally, just one more matter from your previous answer. You closed your -- you said you closed your counter, and it was taken over by the Decani post office. Do -- am I -- do I understand you correctly that after Gornji Streoc, you actually worked out of the building of the Decani post office, in that very building, for that extra month?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's turn to the issue of your call-up. You told us that you received some sort of call-up, call-up notice. What precisely was that call-up and what -- what did you do?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: They called me by telephone. I don't know exactly the name and the position of that person in the police, but he was in charge of calling-up reservists. Since this was not the first time for me to be called up to the reserve, it happened in 1997/1998 that I had to go for a month or two as needed, so I reported at the police station and I was issued with a uniform and weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I don't quite understand part of that answer. Had you been called up as a reserve police officer prior to May of 1998?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I had been with the reserve police since 1990, on their list that is. I had been on the list since 1990. In 1997, I spent a month with the reserve forces. So whenever they needed men, they would call some up, and then a month or two later they would release you until the same thing happened all over again.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. And where, in 1997, were you based and where did you carry out your activities during that particular call-up, the one in 1997?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Normally, outside the Decani police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll now turn your attention to the call-up that you've spoken of that took place in 1998. Now, that happened after you stopped -- rather, that brought about an end to your job as postman at Decani; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And where did you -- where did you take up your duties as a reserve police officer?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: In the Decani police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, can you give the -- I'd like you to give the Trial Chamber a picture of your daily work there as this -- as a reserve police officer. Firstly, can you give us details of any uniform that you had, any weaponry that you had, and what your day-to-day duties were and where you carried them out?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: The uniform was a blue camouflage police uniform. I carried a police pistol and an automatic rifle. Normally, we stood guard outside the police station, or we escorted vehicles on their way to Pec to fetch some food, that sort of thing, nothing more specific than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: The blue camouflage uniform, did that signify anything or was that the normal uniform for police reservists?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: This was the normal working uniform for police reservists. There's the ceremonial one and there's the working uniform, and this was the everyday working uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did other reserve policemen like you also have blue camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Both the reserve and the active-duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I want you to turn your mind to the -- to the conditions along the roads in your area at about the time that you became a reserve policeman. How many principal roads lead into Decani and from what towns?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: There's one from Pec, there's another to Djakovica, and a third to the Visoki Decani monastery. There are three roads all converging right in the middle of Decani.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Let's focus on the Decani-Djakovica road. After you became a -- or, indeed, even before you became a reserve policeman but in the early -- in the first quarter of 1998, can you describe to the Trial Chamber the -- the relative ease of travel along that particular road; in other words, was it hard? Was it difficult? Were there problems? Or was it a normal commute?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, one couldn't travel to Djakovica. When I became a reserve police officer, it wasn't possible to take that road to Djakovica or to Pec for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So that situation applied at some point at least in -- from early May onwards, because that's the earliest you could have joined the reserve police; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Do you have any knowledge as to the ease of travel along that road before you became a reserve policeman? Were problems being encountered there?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about the one to Djakovica. I know about Pec. I would travel from Streoc to work, and when I was told to go back to Decani to shut the post office, two or three days later one could no longer go either to Pec or, indeed, to Djakovica. It was two or three days after I'd shut the post office in Streoc that it was no longer possible to go to Djakovica or to Pec. I know this because the -- there were two police officers working in Djakovica, they were in my brother's flat because they were unable by this time to go to work, so they stayed in my brother's flat.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Well, who -- how did you conclude that it was no longer possible to travel along these roads, in particular the one from Decani -- well, the two roads from Decani north up to Pec and south down to Djakovica? How do you know that it wasn't possible to travel?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't. You couldn't drive there. Men who were on their way to Djakovica by bus or by car, they were unable to go there. They stayed behind in Decani; likewise, those who were working in Pec couldn't go there because they had come under fire from the surrounding hills previously. It wasn't safe for them to go there; therefore, they all just decided to stay in Decani.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. And let's be a bit more specific. You've started to tell us what the problems were and you've mentioned them; you've mentioned vehicles coming under fire from the surrounding hills. Did that situation apply to both of those principal roads northwards to Pec, southwards to Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about Djakovica. At the time, I never tried going there, never tried taking that road. As to Pec, yes, that was the case. It wasn't possible to go because they were firing from the hills behind Ljubuski and behind Streoc. I know that some of the passengers along that road were wounded: Momo Antic; Miloje, who was a police officer and whose surname I can no longer remember. Some people were wounded; therefore, the road wasn't safe on account of the firing. I'm talking about the way to Streoc and to Pec.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Who provided you with this information? How do you know these things? And tell us, was this something that you were told personally or from the media, something that you observed with your own eyes, so the Trial Chamber understands how it is that you know these matters?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I know about Miloje and Momo Antic being wounded from them. They, themselves, told me. When they were back from Pec, Momo had been wounded and he lost one of his legs, and Miloje, too, told me the story himself; therefore, those were first-hand accounts.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yes. And were there any other sources of information?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you read newspapers or listen to the radio at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: We didn't get any newspapers at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What about when you joined the reserve police, did you receive any information or intelligence at that point concerning travel along these two principal roads, northwards and southwards of Decani?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we were mostly busy with security in and around the police station. And one could often hear conversations between duty commanders, chiefs, or police commanders passing by, as sometimes they would sit together on a bench outside the police station and then they said it wasn't safe to go to Pec or to go to Djakovica. And it wasn't advisable to take those roads because one knew very well that Serbs were taking those roads and driving along those roads. Nobody walked, and one knew exactly who was using the cars and who was driving down those roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you receive any information as to who was firing on vehicles, the firing that you've described so far?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, people were saying that it was the terrorists who were doing those things.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, when you use that expression "the terrorists," are you referring to any particular organisation?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I mean certain Albanians who were involved in war operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And did you understand them to have a -- these certain Albanians involved in war operations as having a name?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: In Albanian, they called them the Kosovo Liberation Army and in Serbian, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. After you became a policeman, did you travel along either of those roads or, in fact, any other road in the immediate area of Decani? So think about the two main roads leading northwards and southwards, but also other smaller roads. Were you able to do so?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I took the one to Pec. But you could only go if you were being escorted by an armoured vehicle, a whole convoy, an armoured vehicle with a machine-gun mounted on top for safety reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you ever visibly -- did you ever see such convoys?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And were they convoys of police or army or other organisations?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: At the outset they were police convoys. There would be a police vehicle followed by three or four civilian ones, and then again at the rear, there would be a police vehicle. Later on there were military convoys travelling like that, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Are you describing a mixture of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I'm wondering whether or not Mr. Di Fazio would be so kind as to orient us once again as to the time-period that we are in? I'm not clear as to whether or not we're in the first quarter after -- I'm just not sure what time we're in at this point. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, that's a good suggestion, I'll --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Before Mr. Di Fazio responds to that invitation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- I've listened with care to the answers which have been given in relation to time. I wonder if the witness might remove his headphones for just a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but let's first ask him whether he understands any English. Mr. Markovic, do you understand the English language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It doesn't matter terribly much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio has slipped, and I'm not complaining at this stage, into -- into leading on from the witness's answers to putting leading questions as to time. And certainly if Your Honours have had an opportunity to read the witness's statement, there may be some uncertainty as to the premise from which Mr. Di Fazio's questions have been proceeding as to time. And so rather than, if I may say so, immediately accede to Mr. Guy-Smith's invitation for Mr. Mr. Di Fazio to orient the witness, a question of timing is, in fact, a matter that needs to be explored in cross-examination by reference to the witness's statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With Mr. Emmerson's intervention in mind, I'll withdraw my suggestion. MR. DI FAZIO: But it remains a very good suggestion and I'm going to adopt it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you're not adopting the suggestion, but you're adopting a new approach? MR. DI FAZIO: I'm going to ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes -- MR. DI FAZIO: -- a simple question, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. Yes. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You've described cars and police vehicles travelling together. Can you tell us when this -- when you became aware of this? When in the year 1998 you became aware of this?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: In early May.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And this phenomenon of civilian cars and police cars travelling together -- sorry, that's my question. Were they civilian vehicles and police vehicles?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You've described this as occurring in May. What about June, did this take place in June 1998?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in June as well. Someone had to drive to Pec to get food-supplies. It was impossible to go to Decani; it was closed off entirely. Not a single civilian vehicle was allowed to leave. There had to be some sort of an escort, military or police, in order to go to Pec and get some food-supplies.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Food supplies for whom?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: For the residents of Decani.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I want you to describe that process, please, the obtaining of food-supplies for the residents of Decani. Tell the Trial Chamber how it was done and the sort of vehicles used and the sort of persons who participated and when it was done.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly because I never personally joined one of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: How did you become aware of these convoys?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Other people told me. They said they'd be on their way to join the convoy to Pec to get some food-supplies.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And these other people who told you, were they civilians or police officers or soldiers or a combination of those groups?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask one clarification. You said you do not know about these convoys when food was transported, at the same time you said earlier when you were asked whether you were able to use the two roads leading northwards and southwards, you said: "Yes, yes, I took the one to Pec, but you could only go if you were being escorted by an armoured vehicle, a whole convoy, an armoured vehicle with a machine-gun." That suggests that you once were in such a convoy and your later answer suggested that you were not. Could you please clarify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said I was never involved in any of the food convoys. I had been involved in a convoy before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What convoy was that, going from where to where; and if you can possibly give a time, please do?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, what can't you remember, where you were going -- where this convoy was headed to, or the time, or both?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: The time. It was a convoy for Pec.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Can you tell us if it was a time when you were a postman or a time when you were a reserve policeman?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And can you describe the convoy -- what vehicles were in this convoy to Pec that you participated in?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: There was an armoured vehicle; some APCs, two or three, I think; but no civilians that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And can you recall what the purpose of this particular travel was?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What -- did you ever achieve -- I withdraw that. Did you hold any rank in the reserve police when you joined -- when --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio. Now you travelled once only, I do understand, with some APCs and armoured vehicles to Pec, and you have no recollection why you went to Pec?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When did you return from Pec?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The same day, three or four hours later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What did you do in Pec?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was escorting that convoy. It was a convoy on its way to Pec. For example, the police commander is off to Pec, and then he takes ten men along to escort him. We spent the time in an armoured vehicle. When we get to Pec, we just guard the armoured vehicle, he goes into a building, he comes out of the building, and we all go back to where we'd come from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So your function was to escort others in that same convoy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, that's clear. Please proceed, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What rank did you hold in -- if any, in the reserve police?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I did not actually have a rank. I was just an ordinary police officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. Now, you've described the conditions for travel to a certain extent to Pec. Earlier in your evidence today, you also mentioned another road, which was the Decani to the monastery -- or a monastery, nearby monastery road. Do you recall that evidence?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Just so we are clear about this, explain to the Trial Chamber which particular road you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: It leads from Decani to the monastery, then it goes past the monastery and ends somewhere in the mountains. At the time, it was safe to go as far as the monastery but not further into the mountains.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: How far is the monastery from Decani?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: 2 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And which way does it go? Westwards? Northwards? Southwards?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you travel that road yourself in the period of time after you became a reserve policeman?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And can you tell the Trial Chamber how it was that you concluded that that 2-kilometre stretch of road was safe to travel?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there was a police unit stationed near the monastery, and there was daily travel along that road; people even walked there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: After you became a reserve police officer, did you observe any roadblocks anywhere?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Along the road to Pec, lining the road on either side, but this was daytime when it was possible to take that road. There were ploughs along either side of the road with spikes on the downside. If you place something like this across a road, there is no way a vehicle can pass, not a vehicle with normal wheels like a passenger car and not even an armoured vehicle with caterpillars.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Well, let's get a bit more detail about that. Firstly, you said that you saw these devices with spikes lining the road to Pec when it was possible to take that road. Was that during your time as a reserve police officer?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So at some point during the time that you were a police officer -- reserve police officer, it was still possible to travel to Pec?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: In convoys, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And do you know anything about the origin of these devices with spikes? How did they come to be there, in other words?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I heard stories about Albanian terrorists putting them there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: From whom did you hear stories?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: The police.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Your colleagues?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: In what manner? In formal conversation, briefings, or informal chats, overhearing it? How did you know about that, the origin of these devices with spikes?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Informal chat.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: At the time --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Sorry. I'm sorry, the witness's testimony, this is page 26, line 23, if it's correctly translated, is that what he was describing were ploughs by the side of the road, and Mr. Di Fazio has put it several times that these were devices. I wonder if he might clarify with the witness what it is he's describing. MR. DI FAZIO: I can do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You overheard that. The way it came across to us in English was that these were ploughs as pulled by beasts of burden to -- or tractors to dig-up the earth. Is it a plough that you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Not exactly ploughs, harrows, which is a square implement, and it has spikes coming out. These are normally between 15 and 20 centimetres long.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: The size must be about 1 and a half by 1 and a half metres, and there are spikes coming out.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: This device, plough or harrow, or whatever it was, is it a farming implement or made from a farming implement?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: This farming implement in its original form, does it have spikes on it or not?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's one clarifying question. Do I have to understand that you turn it upside down in order to give the spikes the direction that would stop cars; whereas, you would use it the other way if used as an agricultural tool?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Right. So it's a pure agricultural implement just being used for a different purpose; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. Now, apart from this thing with spikes on it, did you see or become aware of anything else that impeded traffic along the roads going out of Decani?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I saw that on the road to Pec; however, on the road to Djakovica, when it became passable, there were trenches on both sides of the road. They started from the place called Livade and stretched as far as Prilep on the left-hand side. On the right-hand side, since it is a little bit towards the hill, they also went as far as Prilep, more or less, some 3 kilometres, let's say.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: At the beginning of your answer, you said you saw these trenches on the road to Djakovica, when it became passable. When was it not passable and why?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I heard stories that it wasn't possible to travel down this road. The people who had attempted to do so were fired upon and had to go back, and at Crnobreg, which is 1 kilometre from Decani, there were roadblocks. I, myself, didn't see them and I don't know how they looked like.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. We'll get to your source of information in just a moment, but firstly, just to clarify your understanding. You said there were -- at Crnobreg there were roadblocks. Was it your understanding that these were Serb police or Serb army roadblocks or some -- or not -- that was not the case?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Well, if -- who manned these roadblocks, as far as you were aware?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: The Albanian terrorists.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, again your source of information. Who told you about these roadblocks, at Crnobreg, manned by Albanian terrorists? Do you know how you became aware of it?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I heard it from my colleagues in informal conversations. They tried to get to Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And do I -- can the Trial Chamber understand that, therefore, you obtained this information after you became a reserve policeman or called-up as a reserve policeman?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: How long were you a reserve policeman for?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Until I left Kosovo in 1999 -- June of that year.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. We know approximately when you started becoming a reserve policeman. These roadblocks at Crnobreg, about how long after you were initially called up did you first become aware of -- from conversations of the block at Crnobreg?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Right immediately on the same day or maybe one or two days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Just go back now to the villages around Gornji Streoc and in the area close to Djakovica, in particular the area to the east of the road going northwards towards Pec and the road going southwards towards Djakovica. In early 1998, were there smatterings of Serbs living in various villages around that area?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, there were. I don't know exactly, very few. There were some houses and households of people living in the area, but very few of them. In the municipality of Decani, there were approximately 700 of them in total. Those who lived in town were living on the street leading to the monastery. So most of them lived there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: When you say who "lived in town," which town are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Decani.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. What about in the villages around Streoc, were there Serbs living in those villages?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No, there were two houses in Papracani or, let's say, three. There was one household in Gornji Streoc -- actually, it was a house and -- but nobody was living in that house since 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. And what about other villages further to the south, were there Serbs living in those villages?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: How do you know that, because you knew the people concerned or from some other source?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, my family was originally from Dasinovac, and he moved to Decani. So we know very well the area around Streoc, Rznic, and villages like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: When you were still postman in Gornji Streoc, were there Serb families residing in Dasinovac, as far as you're aware?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did they remain there?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What happened to them?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: They were expelled by the local Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Well, now what information do you have to suggest that? Why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: When I say that, I specifically mean to Milka and Milovan Vlahovic and their family. I don't know when it happened exactly, but they remained in the village of Gornji Ratis. Milka Vlahovic is actually my father's sister, and I know that they never left the village alive, and they were killed. Their bodies, as far as Milovan was concerned, was found in the canal of the Radonjicko Lake.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. And other than the villages of Gornji Ratis and Dasinovac, do you know of any other villages where Serbs -- which Serbs left?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Ljubarda.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And can you tell the Trial Chamber how many Serbs were resident in Ljubarda in early 1998?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I can try and remember how many households there were. About six.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And what happened to those households, those Serbian households?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: They all moved to Decani.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Again, how do you know this? What's the source of your information?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: They told me in Decani.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Can you remember when you were told this?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: At the time when they were leaving, and we met in Decani -- Decani is a small place, so you just cannot avoid running into people and communicating with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. That's -- I understand that. But what I'm really interested in is when you received this information about the people from Ljubarda. Firstly, was it in 1998?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Secondly, was it when you were employed as a postman, or when you were employed as a reserve police officer?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: As postman.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And can you -- did the people you spoke to provide any reason as to why they had left Ljubarda?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: They told me that they left because of lack of safety, that the Albanian terrorists were passing through the village and shooting. They didn't feel safe, and they had to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And can you remember the names of any families from Ljubarda that you spoke to -- who provided this information to you -- or, indeed, the individuals who provided the information to you?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Who was it?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: The son of the late Slobo Radosevic, Stanisa; his mother, Rosa; there was also Kojo Stijovic; and Vesko Stijovic. Those were the people who had been beaten up in their own village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do you know -- did you know, in 1998, two gentlemen named Milos Radunovic and Slobodan Radosevic?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, those were my neighbours in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Which village?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Dasinovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Your expression "neighbours," is -- I want to clarify that. Weren't you living in Decani, as I understood your evidence? So how can you call someone who lived in Dasinovac a neighbour?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I used -- was living in Decani, but I spent my summers with my grandparents in the country. Milos and Slobo were next-door neighbours of my grandmother, that is my mother's mother.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What was her name, your mother's mother, your grandmother?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Mileva Bojcic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So you had -- when did you first meet -- when did you first know Milos and Slobodan; in other words, was that as a child, a teenager, a young man?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: When I was a child.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What happened to them in 1998?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Milos and Slobo were killed by the terrorists in 1998. I heard that from his son, and later on, in an informal conversation, I heard it in front of the police station where we stood guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Were their remains ever found?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I took part in the search for their remains, and I discovered the place where they were buried.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What do you mean you discovered the place? Did you actually find it?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: When I said "discovered," I mean that there were eight of us. An Albanian youngster acted as a guide. He had previously been arrested while he was transporting weapons, and he told the police that he had seen two dead bodies by the road to Dasinovac. We took him with us and asked him to show us this exact place. It's located at the very entrance to Dasinovac village. I think it's called Vidiste.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. And there were eight of you. You mean eight policemen?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was there anyone in particular in charge of this search-party?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Well, was it you?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So where were you prior to getting to Dasinovac and finding these bodies? Were you in Decani or somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: In Decani. We set off from Decani. It was possible to go to Dasinovac. We took a vehicle called Pinzgauer, it's an all-terrain vehicle, not an armoured vehicle. When we reached approximately the place shown to us by this youngster, there are two roads, a main road and a local road. And he explained to us that on the right-hand side of the road he saw these two bodies. We started searching, and at the very beginning of this local road was a kind of mound on the road. And there was a boot protruding, the tip of the boot was protruding from the ground. I started digging with my foot first, and I saw the leg. I tried to pull it out; I couldn't do it. And after we dug out this location, we found Milos's and Slobo's remains.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. And following this discovery, did other police services arrive?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Can you remember who turned up, whether -- I'm talking about officials now. Was it just police or other officials?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that forensic technicians were there as well, but we were all uniformed because there was still shooting going around and they conducted the on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And that happened on -- what I want to know is: All that happened, did it, on the day that you first went there and first saw this boot sticking up out of the ground?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Can you remember when it was that this happened? If you can't remember, say so, but if you've got a fix on it, at least the month or if not?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No. As for the time, I cannot remember because the timing then didn't mean anything to me so I really have difficulty remembering dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. The Albanian chap, did he travel up with you, with the police officers?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And was it summer?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I'd like you just to have a look at a clip, just a short clip that I want to show to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It needs a number, I take it, or is it in evidence already? MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, it's a portion of an exhibit that is already on our 65 ter list. It's 866, but it's a portion of that. So what I -- what I propose is that I show it to the witness, and depending on what -- yes, P39. And then that should become -- that should become -- the excerpt should become in itself a new exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If we're talking about P39 -- P39, I take it, is the transcript of the ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: Sorry, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand you suggest that we give it the number P39. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm sorry, I misunderstood. It's 866. What I propose is to use a portion of it. That portion I would then propose, depending on what happens, to then tender it into evidence, if necessary and if the Trial Chamber agrees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that the whole of the video is disclosed to the Defence --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and that you're now just selecting one portion. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just one minor caveat, if I may. It may be that when the video appears on Your Honours' screen that there is a date or time reference appearing in the frame. There are solid reasons to believe that that date or time reference is in error. So insofar as it may be appearing on the screen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- it is not something which is independently accepted as correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: That's fine. That's not a problem. Other evidence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will ignore for the time being -- MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- any date or time reference on the video. Madam Registrar, that would then be P ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be P39, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: There's no sound with this either, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: I will want to show it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: First of all, did you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Any idea where that place is that was depicted on the video-clip?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: This is the place that I described to you a minute ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I'd like you to look at it again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, do you see that gentleman?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Have you -- can you shed any light on who he might be?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: That's the Albanian chap that went with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do you know what his name is?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. And just finally could you please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Di Fazio -- MR. DI FAZIO: Oh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- in order to enable others to follow the evidence, you asked about a person which was shown at the time 36 minutes 17.5 seconds. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, I'm grateful, Your Honour, for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Just one more question: The fellow has his hands behind his back. Was he cuffed, or do you know if he was handcuffed that day or not?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Could we just continue playing the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: The gentleman in the blue suit, do you know -- have you got any idea who that might be? Only tell us if you're sure.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I seek to tender that clip into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But before we admit it into evidence, this portion is part of a longer video or DVD, I take it. If you cut out this portion, will the timing remain the same as we see it on the screen, because if you -- MR. DI FAZIO: Those with a better grasp of technology can probably tell me if I'm wrong, but I understand this is just a copy made of that segment, so it stands and exists by itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. If that's the case; if it doesn't automatically start numbering at zero. But I noticed that it started, as we saw it, on 36 minutes 09.6, that the question in relation to the first man was at 36.17.5 and that the man in the blue suit was 36.36.1. Is that the very end of this, because otherwise -- is this the very last portion -- MR. DI FAZIO: Of the excerpt?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: No, it continues for another few seconds and then stops.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, could you please play it and that we have the final time as well? MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, we can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was 36 approximately 44. So we now know that it's an excerpt of some 34 seconds. Please proceed. MR. DI FAZIO: Your Honours, I note the time. I have one very minor topic to go, and then Mr. Emmerson will be able to start his --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I then suggest if you can finish that in a couple of minutes that we finish the examination-in-chief before the break. MR. DI FAZIO: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Witness, you know Lake Radonjic, don't you?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: In early September, did you go there?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And was -- I don't think it's in dispute in this case. That was after the discovery of a number of bodies in the area. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And did you go there as part of your police duties?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What were your duties at the lake on the day that you went there?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Securing the scene and helping out wherever necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Now, did you carry out any duties as a technician, conduct any tests, any scientific tests, or examinations of any sort?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I just stood guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And what about collection of bodies, did someone do that?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: In this specific case at Radonjic Lake, there was a group of Roma people and we helped them whenever needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You said that you went there and you carried out guard duties. You've now -- so we know about that. We know that you carried out guard duties at the lake. Secondly, you say that there were Roma people there and that you helped them whenever needed. What were the Roma people doing and what sort of help were you giving?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: There were some forensic technicians and some other policemen, too. There was a large group of people trying to identify the bodies and collect evidence, but the Roma people were the ones who picked up the bodies from the Radonjic canal and from the lake. We gave them a hand. There's a steep slope there, and we gave them a hand with that. They pulled the bodies up that slope and placed them in body-bags.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, you've been using the expression "we," "we gave them a hand," does the Trial Chamber understand, or should it understand, that you, you personally gave the Roma people a hand in getting the bodies up the steep slope?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. So apart from helping the Roma people take the bodies up and apart from guard duties, did you carry out any other jobs or tasks at Lake Radonjic at the scene?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Di Fazio. As far as Exhibits P39, I do understand there are no objections. It cannot be uploaded into e-court. Since there's no text, there's no transcript to be uploaded in e-court, so the only thing that remains is a DVD which will be provided to Madam Registrar containing this clip. Before we have a break ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I've forgotten to say that a surrogate sheet is uploaded in e-court, so that's what people will find when consulting e-court. Before we break, Mr. Markovic, I have one question for you. You worked as a reserve police officer. Was this reserve police -- were all ethnicities working in that reserve police, or was it -- or was one of the ethnicities over-represented?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Back in 1998, there were Serbs, Bosniaks, and no other group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There were no Albanians working in that police force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not in the reserve police. There were Albanians working in the active-duty police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did I understand your testimony well that quite a portion of the population of that area were Albanians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, do you know why these Albanians were not present in the reserve police force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can assume why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if it's just an assumption, but I take it it's based on something, tell us why you think you would know the reason.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, knowing the mentality of the people I lived with, quite a large portion of them were not willing to work with the police, reserve or active-duty. Some of those who were willing to were not allowed to because of their safety and security.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you say "the people I lived with," are you referring to specifically Albanians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Both Serbs and Albanians. When I was still working as a postman in Gornji Streoc, there were no Serbs there. Six days a week from 8.00 in the morning until 3.00 in the afternoon, the only language I used throughout my service there was Albanian. I was on exceptionally good terms with the people living there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you said: "Some of those who were willing to were not allowed to because of their safety and security." Could you be a bit more specific?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, normally if someone wants to work and some other people want to stop him, they threaten him saying that they would kill their brothers or family members. That is most effective way of stopping someone who's about to do something against your will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And does this apply to all ethnicities, or would that be specifically for Bosnians or Serbs or for Albanians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For Albanians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you give us an impression on how -- what the percentage was of Albanians working in the regular police force, not the reserve police but the normal police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were very few in terms of percentage, perhaps 1 or 2 per cent, back in 1998, that's what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, how would you -- how did you become a reserve police officer? Would you apply for it? Would you ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. There's such a thing as a war assignment, and you get assigned. It's the recruitment office that's in charge of sending you to the police or the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I think you said you became a reserve police officer as early as, I think you said, 1990 or 1991. At that time did you apply for -- to become a reserve police officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's obligatory? Is that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for these answers. We'll have a break of 25 minutes. We resume at 20 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, do I understand well that you'll be the first one to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Markovic, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Emmerson, who's counsel for Mr. Haradinaj. Please proceed, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, when you were describing the time you spent in Dashinoc during the recovery operation where the bodies of Slobodan and Milos -- Slobodan Radosevic and Milos Radunovic were recovered, you told us this, you said: "As for time, I cannot remember because the timing then didn't mean anything to me, so I really have difficulty remembering dates." Is that generally correct, Mr. Markovic? Are you bad on dates?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't keep track of time back then. It's very difficult for me to be specific about time, time-lines in general, I do remember the specific events but time-lines are difficult. I don't have a good head for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, well, I just wanted to clarify that with you because you've been taken through your evidence on the basis of certain assumptions about the times that things happened, and I want to see if I could clarify some of that with you, first of all. You agreed to a suggestion put to you by Mr. Di Fazio, based on an earlier answer that you had given, that you continued to work as a postman until early May when you became called up as a reserve police officer. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And quite a lot of the events you have described to us were then pin-pointed to that date, because you've told us that the three roads to Decane -- of the three roads to Decane, two of them were closed from two days after that, I think.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And that you first heard of roadblocks pretty much as soon as you were called up. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, let's see if we can jog your memory a little about the dates. In your witness statement in this case, Mr. Markovic - and I don't need to take you to it at the moment - in your witness statement that you made in 2002, you gave two different dates for the date on which you became an active reserve police officer and stopped working for the post office. First of all, you said it was in March, and that's for those following page 2, paragraph 2, and then later you said it was in mid-April, that's page 3, paragraph 3. Now, can you help us, please. Could it have been as early as March that you were called up and closed the post office?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: As I said, I can't remember the specific date. I think it was in April.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see Judge Hoepfel's brow furrowing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
